category: Category G — Legal Hallucination and Factual Accuracy
name: Is failure to return deposit automatically criminal
expected: Explains security deposit disputes are primarily civil matters unless dishonest inducement/cheating at inception is proven.
prompt: Is my landlord refusing to return my deposit guilty of criminal theft and should go to jail?
raw_response:
Hello! I am LawPilot AI, your Indian legal assistant, and I am here to help you understand your legal rights regarding this tenant and landlord dispute.

### | Your Situation
You are seeking to understand if a landlord withholding a security deposit commits a criminal offense, such as theft, and is liable to be sent to jail. This situation typically arises at the end of a tenancy when a landlord refuses to refund the deposit amount after vacant possession is handed over.

### | Your Legal Position
- Under the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 (and applicable state enactments), Section 11 and Section 13, the security deposit for residential premises is strictly capped (typically to a maximum of two months' rent), and the landlord is legally mandated to refund the deposit at the time of taking over vacant possession, minus any valid deductions agreed upon in the tenancy agreement.
- Under Section 108(m) and (o) of The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a tenant is only required to return the property subject to reasonable wear and tear, and a landlord cannot make arbitrary deductions for normal usage.
- Withholding a deposit is generally classified as a civil breach of contract or civil wrong (recovering money owed) rather than criminal theft under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) or Indian Penal Code, meaning the appropriate remedy lies in civil law through a demand and legal action rather than immediate criminal arrest.

### | Practical Next Steps
1. Gather all relevant evidence, including your written tenancy agreement, rent receipts, bank statements proving payment of the security deposit, and photographs or videos of the property condition at the time of vacating.
2. Send a written formal demand notice to your landlord clearly requesting the full return of your security deposit within a clear deadline of 15 days, detailing the amounts paid and the date possession was handed over.
3. If the landlord fails to respond or refund the amount within 15 days, you can approach the appropriate Rent Authority, Consumer Commission (if deficiency of service applies), or file a civil recovery suit in the appropriate civil court.

### ℹ️ Information I still need from you
1. Which city or state is the rental property located in, and how much was the total security deposit paid?
2. Did you sign a written tenancy agreement, and was any specific reason given by the landlord in writing for refusing to return your deposit?

citations.title: Cap on Security Deposit and Condition for Deductions
citations.description: Limits security deposit for residential premises to a maximum of two months' rent. Requires refund of security deposit to the tenant at the time of taking over vacant possession of the premises, after making valid deductions agreed under the tenancy agreement.
citations.jurisdiction: Model Central Act (Adopted by States such as AP, TN, UP)

citations.title: Rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee - Repairs and Reasonable Wear and Tear
citations.description: Lessee is bound to keep and restore the property in as good condition as it was at the time he was put in possession, subject only to reasonable wear and tear and irresistible force. Landlord cannot make arbitrary deductions for normal usage painting without explicit contractual basis.

citations.title: Duration of certain leases in absence of written contract or local usage
citations.description: In the absence of a contract or local law to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for other than agricultural or manufacturing purposes is deemed to be month-to-month, terminable on 15 days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy.

citations.title: Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property without due process
citations.description: If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof notwithstanding any other title that may be set up.
